title: How To End Each Day On The Right Classroom Management Foot m-management-foot/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the final ten to fifteen minutes of the school day are often mishandled, producing chaos that colors students' overall impression of the classroom. He lays out a detailed dismissal routine: pausing for thirty seconds to reset, having students clean up their own space, checking homework readiness, personally distributing handouts, packing backpacks in small groups, observing one minute of silence, and lining up row by row to walk to a consistent dismissal spot. He stresses that, like any routine, this sequence must be taught and practiced thoroughly before it can run smoothly, and closes with the image of ending each day with a fist bump or handshake as a small ritual of connection.
points: The final 10-15 minutes of the school day are identified as a common trouble spot that shapes students' overall impression of the classroom.
The recommended dismissal routine includes a 30-second pause, student-led cleanup, a homework readiness check, personal handout distribution, and a full minute of silence.
Handouts should be distributed by the teacher directly, not through mailboxes or student jobs, to ensure they actually reach home.
Homework should never be assigned or explained during the final minutes of the day — that should happen earlier, right after the related lesson.
The routine must be explicitly taught and practiced, like any other, before it can run efficiently and calmly.
quotes: This is why it’s so common to see misbehavior at dismissal—swinging backpacks, chasing, shouting, pushing, roughhousing…students wound up and tuned out, oblivious to your warnings and exhortations.
The problem with this, beyond the immediate chaos and misbehavior, is that students strongly associate the last few minutes of the day with the culture of your classroom.

Homework should be assigned, explained, and checked for understanding earlier in the day and immediately following your lesson (on the homework topic). It should never, ever be shoehorned in at the end of the day.

By making the last 10-15 minutes of each day a choreographed routine, you’ll have zero behavior problems, your students will be much better prepared to complete their homework, and you’ll guarantee yourself a pleasant ending to every school day.
When you arrive with your class at your predetermined goodbye spot, make it a point to bump fists or shake hands with each student, in modest celebration of another great day.
